questions.question: How many files in this repo READ `main.dbdemos_ecom.orders_raw`, which files are they, and is there anything unusual about how one of them reads it relative to the medallion (bronze->silver->gold) layering?
questions.reference_answer: Two files read `orders_raw`: (1) `silver/orders_cleaned.py` via `spark.table(f"{database}.orders_raw")`, and (2) `silver/customer_profile.py` via `spark.table(f"{database}.orders_raw")` (one of its three bronze reads). The unusual part: `silver/customer_profile.py` reads the BRONZE `orders_raw` table directly rather than the already-cleaned SILVER `orders_cleaned` table produced by `silver/orders_cleaned.py`. So the two silver files both consume bronze orders independently — customer_profile bypasses the cleaning/filtering done in orders_cleaned (e.g. the status!='cancelled' & quantity>0 filter and the type normalizations), operating on the raw bronze rows instead.

questions.question: Which file produces `main.dbdemos_ecom.events_raw`, and is the write a streaming write or a batch write? Name the write format and trigger.
questions.reference_answer: `bronze/03_ingest_events.py` produces `main.dbdemos_ecom.events_raw`. It is a STREAMING write: `events_final.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", f"{checkpoint_root}/events").option("mergeSchema","true").trigger(availableNow=True).table(f"{database}.events_raw")`. Format is Delta; the trigger is `availableNow=True` (process the accumulated backlog once, then stop — a batch-flavored streaming trigger). The source is an Auto Loader (`cloudFiles`) read stream over the events landing path.

questions.question: Trace the lineage of `gold.product_performance.order_count` back to its originating bronze source. Name the aggregation, the intermediate table, and the bronze table/column.
questions.reference_answer: `order_count` is produced in `gold/product_performance.py` by `F.count("order_id").alias("order_count")` inside `daily_perf = orders.groupBy("product_id", "order_date").agg(*aggregations, F.count("order_id").alias("order_count"))`. Its input `orders` is `spark.table(f"{database}.orders_cleaned")` — the SILVER table. `silver/orders_cleaned.py` produces `orders_cleaned` from `spark.table(f"{database}.orders_raw")` (BRONZE). The `order_id` column is a passthrough from `orders_raw` (it is never re-derived in orders_cleaned). So the chain is: `bronze orders_raw.order_id` -> (read + cleaned, order_id unchanged) `silver orders_cleaned.order_id` -> `count(order_id)` grouped by product_id/order_date -> `gold product_performance.order_count`. orders_raw itself is ingested from the JSON landing volume by `bronze/01_ingest_orders.py`.

questions.question: `gold/product_performance.py` groups by `order_date`, but `order_date` is not a column in any bronze table. Where does `order_date` come from, and what is its full derivation chain back to bronze?
questions.reference_answer: `order_date` is a SILVER-derived column, created in `silver/orders_cleaned.py` by `.withColumn("order_date", F.to_date(F.col("order_ts")))`. Its input `order_ts` is a bronze `orders_raw` column (passed through; never re-derived). So the chain is: `bronze orders_raw.order_ts` (ingested from the JSON landing volume by `bronze/01_ingest_orders.py`) -> `silver/orders_cleaned.py`: `order_date = to_date(order_ts)` -> written to `silver orders_cleaned.order_date` -> read by `gold/product_performance.py` as a groupBy key. Note `order_year` and `order_month` are also derived from `order_ts` in the same file, but only `order_date` is consumed downstream (as the product_performance group key); the year/month columns are not used by any other file.

questions.question: If `order_ts` were renamed in `bronze.orders_raw`, list every downstream column (across silver and gold) that would break or need updating.
questions.reference_answer:
`order_ts` feeds several derivations across two readers of orders_raw:
(1) In `silver/orders_cleaned.py` it derives THREE columns: `order_date = to_date(order_ts)`, `order_year = year(order_ts)`, `order_month = month(order_ts)`.
(2) In `silver/customer_profile.py` (which reads orders_raw directly) it is used in the aggregation `F.max("order_ts").alias("last_order_ts")`, producing `customer_profile.last_order_ts`.
Transitively in gold:
(3) `gold/customer_ltv.py` selects `last_order_ts` from customer_profile and derives `days_since_last_order = DATEDIFF(CURRENT_DATE(), last_order_ts)`; both `last_order_ts` and `days_since_last_order` would break.
(4) `gold/product_performance.py` groups by `order_date` (the silver-derived column), so its grouping/key would break.
Summary of affected columns: orders_cleaned.{order_date, order_year, order_month}; customer_profile.last_order_ts; customer_ltv.{last_order_ts, days_since_last_order}; and the product_performance group-by key order_date.

questions.question: If `total_amount` were renamed in `bronze.orders_raw`, trace the full downstream blast radius across silver and gold, including any gold columns affected only transitively.
questions.reference_answer:
`total_amount` is consumed by both readers of orders_raw:
(1) `silver/orders_cleaned.py`: `.withColumn("total_amount", F.round(F.col("total_amount"), 2))` (re-derives the same name) and `.withColumn("is_high_value", F.col("total_amount") > F.lit(1000))`. Both `orders_cleaned.total_amount` and `orders_cleaned.is_high_value` break.
(2) `silver/customer_profile.py` (reads orders_raw directly): `F.sum("total_amount").alias("lifetime_revenue")` -> `customer_profile.lifetime_revenue` breaks.
Transitive gold impact via lifetime_revenue in `gold/customer_ltv.py`: `lifetime_revenue` is selected into the `base` CTE and then drives `country_avg.avg_country_ltv = AVG(lifetime_revenue)`, `ltv_vs_country_avg = lifetime_revenue / NULLIF(avg_country_ltv,0)`, `revenue_quartile = NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_revenue DESC)`, and therefore `ltv_tier` (the categorical label derived from revenue_quartile). So customer_ltv.{lifetime_revenue, avg_country_ltv, ltv_vs_country_avg, revenue_quartile, ltv_tier} are all affected.
Note on product_performance: it aggregates a runtime-loaded `metric_columns` list (dynamic, opaque). If `total_amount` is one of those metrics it would also be affected there, but that cannot be determined statically.

questions.question: In `silver/customer_profile.py` the first join is `customers_df.join(orders_df, on="customer_id", how="inner")`. If this were changed from `inner` to `left`, what changes semantically in the output, and what changes (if anything) in the lineage graph structure?
questions.reference_answer:
Semantic change: with `inner`, customers who have NO matching rows in orders_raw are dropped entirely from the profile. With `left`, every customer is retained; for customers with no orders the order-side columns (order_id, total_amount, order_ts, product_id, ...) come through NULL. Downstream that changes the aggregates: `F.count("order_id")` becomes 0 for order-less customers (count ignores nulls), `F.sum("total_amount")` (lifetime_revenue) becomes NULL, `F.max("order_ts")` (last_order_ts) NULL, and `F.countDistinct("product_id")` 0. Those order-less customers then flow into gold/customer_ltv with NULL lifetime_revenue, affecting avg_country_ltv, ltv_vs_country_avg (NULL), and the NTILE revenue_quartile ranking.
Lineage graph structure: the join is still one Joins edge between the same two inputs on the same key (customer_id); only the join-TYPE attribute changes from inner to left. No nodes/edges are added or removed — it is a property change on the existing join edge, not a structural change.

questions.question: If the row filter `.filter((F.col("status") != "cancelled") & (F.col("quantity") > 0))` in `silver/orders_cleaned.py` were removed, which downstream tables' values would change and which would NOT — and why?
questions.reference_answer:
Removing the filter lets cancelled orders and zero-quantity orders pass into `silver orders_cleaned`. Impact:
- CHANGES: `gold/product_performance.py`, because it reads `orders_cleaned` and aggregates it (sums/avgs/maxes per product per day plus count(order_id)); those metrics would now include the previously-filtered cancelled/zero-qty rows.
- DOES NOT change: `silver/customer_profile.py` and therefore `gold/customer_ltv.py`. Crucially, customer_profile reads the BRONZE `orders_raw` table directly, NOT `orders_cleaned`, so it never saw this filter in the first place — its aggregates (total_orders, lifetime_revenue, etc.) are computed over unfiltered bronze orders regardless. (Note: in the lineage graph the removal also deletes the Filters edge on the orders_cleaned pipeline; no other structural change.)

questions.question: If the `email` column were dropped from `bronze.customers_raw`, which downstream silver and gold columns are affected, and is the impact computational or merely structural (passthrough)?
questions.reference_answer: `email` is read by `silver/customer_profile.py` and used ONLY as one of the group-by grain keys: `.groupBy("customer_id", "email", "country_code", "signup_ts")`. It is carried as an output attribute of `customer_profile` but is never used in any computed expression. In `gold/customer_ltv.py`, `email` is selected through the `base` CTE and passed through `ranked` to the final SELECT (and into the written `customer_ltv` table) — again pure passthrough, no computation depends on it. So the affected columns are `customer_profile.email` and `customer_ltv.email`. The impact is structural/passthrough only: removing it drops a grain attribute and a passthrough column, but changes no aggregation result, no derived value, and no join (the joins key on customer_id / country_code, not email). No numeric or categorical output (lifetime_revenue, quartile, tier, etc.) changes.

questions.question: What is the grain (set of group-by keys) of the aggregation in `silver/customer_profile.py`, what are all of its aggregate output columns, and what is unusual about including `signup_ts` as a grain key?
questions.reference_answer: The aggregation is `profile.groupBy("customer_id", "email", "country_code", "signup_ts").agg(...)`. Grain keys: customer_id, email, country_code, signup_ts (four keys). Aggregate outputs (five): `total_orders = count(order_id)`, `lifetime_revenue = sum(total_amount)`, `last_order_ts = max(order_ts)`, `last_event_ts = max(event_ts_last_event)`, `distinct_products_ordered = countDistinct(product_id)`. What is unusual: the effective grain is one row per customer (customer_id is the natural key); email, country_code, and signup_ts are functionally dependent on customer_id and are included in the group-by only to carry them through to the output as attributes (a common Spark idiom since non-aggregated columns must appear in groupBy). Including `signup_ts` — a timestamp — as a grain key is notable because if a customer ever had two different signup_ts values it would split into multiple rows; it works here only on the assumption signup_ts is constant per customer.

questions.question: The aggregation in `gold/product_performance.py` is `.agg(*aggregations, F.count("order_id").alias("order_count"))`. Which portion of this aggregation can a static analyzer enumerate and which cannot, what are the group keys, and what determines the unresolvable portion?
questions.reference_answer: Group keys: `product_id` and `order_date` (`orders.groupBy("product_id", "order_date")`). The aggregation has two portions: (1) STATICALLY ENUMERABLE: `F.count("order_id").alias("order_count")` — a fixed, literal aggregate producing `order_count`. (2) NOT ENUMERABLE: `*aggregations`, a star-unpacked Python list built at runtime by a loop `for col_name in metric_columns: aggregations.append(F.sum(col_name)...); .append(F.avg(col_name)...); .append(F.max(col_name)...)`. The list contents depend on `metric_columns`, which is loaded from an out-of-repo JSON file: `config_path = os.environ.get("METRIC_CONFIG_PATH", "/dbfs/configs/metrics.json")` then `json.load(f)["product_performance"]`. Neither the env var nor the JSON file contents are resolvable from the code, so the analyzer cannot know how many metrics or which column names. A correct static representation is ONE aggregation step with the known `order_count` output plus an unresolved/dynamic marker for the sum/avg/max-per-metric portion (3 aggregates per unknown metric column).

questions.question: In `silver/customer_profile.py`, if `event_ts` were renamed in `bronze.events_raw`, what specifically breaks in the latest-event window logic and in the downstream aggregation? Account for the suffix-rename step.
questions.reference_answer: Two things break. (1) The window itself: `events_window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("event_ts").desc())` orders by `event_ts`; renaming the source column breaks the ORDER BY key, so `events_ranked = events_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(events_window))` and the subsequent `filter(rn==1)` (latest event per customer) would fail or pick the wrong row. (2) The downstream aggregate: after `events_latest` is suffix-renamed via `rename_columns_with_suffix(events_latest, "_last_event")`, every column gets `_last_event` appended, so `event_ts` becomes `event_ts_last_event`. That suffixed column is consumed by `F.max("event_ts_last_event").alias("last_event_ts")` in the final aggregation. So renaming `event_ts` breaks the window order key, the row_number dedup, AND the `last_event_ts` output column (transitively, customer_ltv.last_event_ts which is a passthrough of it). Note the join key on the events side is `customer_id_last_event` (from customer_id), not event_ts, so the join itself is unaffected.

questions.question: Based on the body of `DeltaMergeSink.run()` in `utils/sinks.py`, what does the sink do on the very first run (when the target table does not yet exist) versus on subsequent runs, and what columns/keys drive the merge?
questions.reference_answer: `DeltaMergeSink.run(df)` branches on whether the target already exists: `if not spark.catalog.tableExists(self.target_table): df.write.format("delta").saveAsTable(self.target_table); return`. So on the FIRST run (table absent) it simply creates the table with a plain Delta `saveAsTable` — no merge. On SUBSEQUENT runs (table exists) it performs a MERGE: `target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, self.target_table)`, builds the match condition by joining the merge keys (`" AND ".join(f"t.{k} = s.{k}" for k in self.merge_keys)`), then `target.alias("t").merge(df.alias("s"), condition).whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()` — i.e. update matched rows in place and insert new ones (SCD-Type-1 upsert). An optional `update_condition` (default None) can gate the `whenMatchedUpdateAll`. For `gold/product_performance.py` the merge keys are `["product_id", "order_date"]`, so matching is on `t.product_id = s.product_id AND t.order_date = s.order_date`.

questions.question: What is the fully-qualified target table written by the `DeltaMergeSink` in `gold/product_performance.py`, and how is that FQN assembled from the repo's configuration?
questions.reference_answer: The sink is constructed as `DeltaMergeSink(target_table=f"{database}.product_performance", merge_keys=["product_id", "order_date"], mode="merge")`. The `database` symbol comes from the setup notebook (imported via `%run ../_resources/setup`), where `database = f"{catalog}.{db}"`, and `catalog = "main"`, `db = "dbdemos_ecom"` come from `config.py`. So `database` = `main.dbdemos_ecom`, and the resolved target FQN is `main.dbdemos_ecom.product_performance`. Write mode is `merge`; merge keys are product_id and order_date.

questions.question: `silver/customer_profile.py` reads `main.dbdemos_ecom.customers_raw`. Is `customers_raw` produced by any file in this repo? What does the answer imply for the lineage of customer-attribute columns like `country_code` and `signup_ts`?
questions.reference_answer: No file in this repo produces `customers_raw`. The only bronze producers are `bronze/01_ingest_orders.py` (writes `orders_raw`) and `bronze/03_ingest_events.py` (writes `events_raw`). There is no `*_ingest_customers` notebook. Therefore `customers_raw` is an EXTERNAL / upstream source as far as this repo is concerned — an orphan input with no in-repo producer. Implication: the lineage of customer-attribute columns sourced from it (e.g. `country_code`, `signup_ts`, `email`, `customer_id`) terminates at `customers_raw` with no further upstream node inside the repo; the graph cannot trace them back to a landing volume or ingest job the way it can for orders (orders_raw <- 01_ingest_orders) and events (events_raw <- 03_ingest_events). A lineage/coverage report should flag customers_raw as a read-but-not-produced (external) table.

questions.question: `bronze/03_ingest_events.py` calls `parse_event_payload(events_landing)`. What does that helper actually do to the schema, and why can a purely static lineage extractor not represent the resulting column-level lineage without extra configuration?
questions.reference_answer: In `utils/event_parsers.py`, `parse_event_payload(df)` parses the JSON `payload` column with a fixed schema (`page_url`, `referrer`, `user_agent`, `cart_total`, all string) via `F.from_json(F.col("payload"), _PAYLOAD_SCHEMA)` into a temporary `_parsed` struct, then adds four new top-level columns — `page_url`, `referrer`, `user_agent`, and `cart_total` (the last cast to `decimal(18,2)`) — and finally drops `_parsed` and the original `payload`. So the net schema change is: one column out (`payload`), four columns in. A static extractor sees only the call site `events_parsed = parse_event_payload(events_landing)` — a call to an imported function. Because this helper is NOT registered in `.degraph/helpers.json` (unlike the column_transformations helpers), the extractor cannot know the column set changed or how; it must represent the step as an opaque transform that preserves the DataFrame's identity but with unknown column-level effects, and emit a warning naming the unregistered helper. Consequently the four parsed columns flowing into `events_raw` have no static column-level provenance back through the payload.

questions.question: If the `lifetime_revenue` aggregation in `silver/customer_profile.py` were changed from `F.sum("total_amount")` to `F.avg("total_amount")`, which gold-tier values in `customer_ltv` would change, and would the lineage graph structure change?
questions.reference_answer: `lifetime_revenue` is consumed extensively in `gold/customer_ltv.py`, so changing its meaning (sum -> avg) ripples through all values computed from it: (1) the `base` CTE selects `lifetime_revenue` (now an average), (2) `country_avg.avg_country_ltv = AVG(lifetime_revenue)` becomes an average-of-averages, (3) `ltv_vs_country_avg = lifetime_revenue / NULLIF(avg_country_ltv, 0)` changes, (4) `revenue_quartile = NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_revenue DESC)` re-ranks customers (so quartile assignments can move), and (5) `ltv_tier` (platinum/gold/silver/bronze derived from revenue_quartile) can change accordingly. The written `customer_ltv.lifetime_revenue` value itself also changes. Lineage graph structure: NO structural change — the aggregate edge still maps `total_amount -> lifetime_revenue`; only the aggregation operator on that edge changes (sum -> avg). Same nodes, same edges, same downstream wiring; only values shift.

questions.question: The column `is_high_value` is derived in `silver/orders_cleaned.py`. Is it consumed by any other file in the repo? Justify your answer from what the downstream consumers actually read.
questions.reference_answer: Statically, `is_high_value` has NO downstream consumer in this repo. It is derived in `silver/orders_cleaned.py` as `.withColumn("is_high_value", F.col("total_amount") > F.lit(1000))` and written into `silver orders_cleaned`. The only file that reads `orders_cleaned` is `gold/product_performance.py`, which groups by `product_id` and `order_date` and aggregates `count(order_id)` plus a runtime `*aggregations` list — none of which references `is_high_value` by name. (customer_profile and customer_ltv do not read orders_cleaned at all.) The one caveat: `product_performance`'s metric list is loaded dynamically from an out-of-repo JSON, so it is conceivable `is_high_value` appears there, but that cannot be confirmed statically. On the evidence in the code, `is_high_value` is effectively a leaf / unused derived column.

questions.question: If the write in `silver/orders_cleaned.py` were changed from `.mode("overwrite")` to `.mode("append")`, would the lineage graph change? Distinguish between what changes in the graph versus what changes in runtime behavior.
questions.reference_answer: Lineage GRAPH: essentially no structural change. The Writes edge from the orders_cleaned pipeline to the `main.dbdemos_ecom.orders_cleaned` table still exists with the same source DataFrame and target table; only the write-mode attribute on that edge changes from `overwrite` to `append` (and the `overwriteSchema=true` option becomes irrelevant for append). No nodes or edges are added/removed, and no column-level lineage changes — every consumer still reads the same table with the same schema. RUNTIME behavior: significant — `overwrite` replaces the table contents each run, whereas `append` accumulates rows across runs, so duplicates would build up (the orders_cleaned pipeline has no dedup/merge), inflating the downstream `product_performance` aggregates. So this is a write-semantics change captured only as a mode property in the graph, not a lineage-structure change.

questions.question: Trace the inputs of `gold.customer_ltv.days_since_last_order` back through the pipeline, and identify any source of non-determinism in its value.
questions.reference_answer: `days_since_last_order` is computed in `gold/customer_ltv.py`'s `ranked` CTE as `DATEDIFF(CURRENT_DATE(), b.last_order_ts) AS days_since_last_order`. Its inputs: `last_order_ts` comes from the `base` CTE, which selects it from `main.dbdemos_ecom.customer_profile`. In `silver/customer_profile.py`, `last_order_ts = F.max("order_ts")` over each customer's joined orders; `order_ts` is a bronze `orders_raw` column (read directly by customer_profile), ingested by `bronze/01_ingest_orders.py`. So the data chain is: `bronze orders_raw.order_ts` -> `customer_profile.last_order_ts = max(order_ts)` -> `customer_ltv.days_since_last_order = DATEDIFF(CURRENT_DATE(), last_order_ts)`. Non-determinism: the `CURRENT_DATE()` term makes the value depend on the DATE THE JOB RUNS — the same input data yields a different `days_since_last_order` on different run dates. This is a run-time-dependent (non-reproducible across days) column, unlike the purely data-derived columns around it.
